They were black, but I made sure none of them turned gray/ashy. Any tips on how to save this? Or if it's beyond salvageable this time, any tips for next time? This was my process: 9 dried guajillo chiles 5 dried ancho chiles 3 morita or chipotle chiles 1 whole head garlic (cloves separated, unpeeled) 1/2 white onion 1/2 cup neutral oil 3 tbsp apple cider vinegar 2 tbsp piloncillo or dark brown sugar 3 tsp salt Water to thin Char the peppers on a dry carbon steel pan until black, soak for about 15min in warm water, char the garlic and onion, blend everything together

Crispy crust banana bread made with mayo. I tried making a mayonnaise banana bread in NOT my kitchen one time but I ended up having to use a toaster oven because the oven was having issues. The resulting banana bread had a beautifully crispy crust which I imagine was because of the close proximity to the heating elements turning on and off. Is there anyway I could recreate this in a regular oven? I tried to do some broiling one time and just burned the shit out of it. Otherwise I'm seriously considering just buying a big ass toaster oven and just trying that. Not sure of the recipe I used because this was in 2019 but it was probably something like this. • 250 g (about 3 large or 1.5 cups) very ripe mashed bananas • 200 g (about 1 packed cup) brown sugar • 1/2 cup (115 g) real mayonnaise • 1 large room-temperature egg • 1 tsp vanilla extract • 220 g (1.5 cups) all-purpose flour • 2 tsp baking powder (or 1 tsp baking soda) • 1/2 tsp salt • 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon (optional) Mix wet, mix dry, combine with as little mixing as possible and bake at 350 in a loaf pan.

Stainless steel Demeyere pan cleaning. Good day, Yesterday, we used our new pan for the first time. I realize now that the pan was likely not hot enough because the water sizzled but didn’t "dance", which I learned after watching several YouTube videos. We prepared a dish called menemen, using 500g of minced meat and six eggs. During cooking, the bottom of the pan became slightly sticky, but with some water and the moisture from the sauce, it cleaned up while cooking. Toward the end, we added two raw eggs on top and let it sit with the lid on for 5/10 minutes. After finishing the dish, we noticed the bottom looked like the attached picture. Here’s what we tried: Boiled water with vinegar and one packet of baking soda for 20 minutes, then let it sit for an hour. this helped somewhat. Repeated the same process, this time boiling for 30 minutes on low heat and soaking overnight. The result was much improved, but not fully clean. Did we do something wrong, or is this normal for a first use? I’ve also ordered Bar Keepers Friend Cookware Cleaner, which hasn’t arrived yet. Will that help? And is it safe to use regularly? I’m still learning and would appreciate any advice. Thank you. Kind regards

Can Tripe be substituted? I am interested in trying out this recipe and am wondering if and how the Tripe could be substituted: (I know that the Tripe is the main ingredient of this dish, but I can’t get any, where I live.) TRIPE À LA CREOLE This tripe stew was widely served in New Orleans in the nineteenth century; it is still prepared at home today. The tripe is simmered in a courtbouillon enriched with beel stock until tender, then added to the sauce and cooked a bit longer. Cleaned, partily precooked tripe is avalable in many of the better markets across the country, and shortens preparation time considerably. Don't overcook the tripe; it should have a pleasant chewy texture. Serve with boiled rice to soak up the heady sauce. (for 4) COURTBOUILLON 3 qt. water, approximately 1 tsp. cayenne 1⅔ Tbs. salt ¼ tsp. finely minced garlic 1 Tbs. white wine vinegar 2 Tbs. rich beef stock (if you have none ½/ onion, cut into quarters on hand use beef concentrate) ½2 tsp. freshly ground black pepper 2½ to 3 lb. honeycomb tripe 2 Tbs. salt butter 2 medium-sized onions, sliced (about 3 с.) ½ c. chopped green pepper ¾ tsp. finely minced garlic ½2 c. finely chopped seasoning ham (about ¼ lb.) 2 whole bay leaves, crushed SAUCE 2 Tbs. minced fresh parsley 1 tsp. dried thyme 1¾ tsp. salt ¾ tsp. freshly ground black pepper 1 tsp. cayenne ¼ tsp. dried basil 2 one-lb. cans peeled whole tomatoes, undrained Boiled Rice (page 17) In a heavy 5- to 6-quart saucepan, combine the ingredients for the courtbouillon. Bring to a boil over high heat, then add the tripe. Reduce the heat to low and cook for 2 to 3 hours, or until the tripe is tender. Meanwhile, in another heavy saucepan about 4 to 5 quarts in capacity melt the butter over low heat. Add the sliced onions and sauté until soft, then add all the other ingredients except the tripe. Continue sautéing for 20 minutes more, stiring frequently. Remove the tripe from the courtbouillon and drain: Allow to cool slightly before handling, then cut into pieces about 2 inches long and ½ inch wide. Add to the pan with the sauce, cover, and cook the tripe in the sauce for 25 minutes. Serve with boiled rice.
